results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: The Virtual Fly Brain database indicates that there are multiple types of Kenyon cells in the adult Drosophila brain. VFB records show subclasses of [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"), including [[KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain")(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), KCab-c, [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Kenyon cell of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, VFB data suggests that Kenyon cells can be further categorized into alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, with subtypes such as core, surface, posterior, anterior-posterior, middle, dorsal, and claw-count classes. VFB holds [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") records of subclasses of Kenyon cell, as well as other relevant data, including images, scRNAseq data, transgene expression, and connectivity classes.

The specific identities and characteristics of these neurons are not specified here, but the data suggests that there are numerous neurons with presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body, which could be considered as main input neurons. For more detailed information, further queries can be made to explore the specific types and Lineage clones found in mushroom body, as well as Expression patterns overlapping mushroom body, which VFB has annotated [34](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,LineageClonesIn "Run in VFB: Lineage clones found in mushroom body") and [23](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,ExpressionOverlapsHere "Run in VFB: Expression patterns overlapping mushroom body") records for, respectively.

results.title: Neuroanatomy
results.question: What brain regions does the antennal lobe connect to?
results.response: The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") connects to the mushroom body and lateral horn, according to the VFB database. More specifically, VFB records show that antennal lobe projection neurons send synaptic output to the mushroom body calyx and/or lateral horn. results.title: Circuit motif
results.question: Describe the dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs). Which DAN types connect to which MBON types?
results.response:
The dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) comes from adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons. VFB holds data on the upstream connectivity classes for MBONs, with [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") records, and for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons, with [1290](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") records. The downstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons are also available, with [316](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") records. 

To determine which [adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049839 "Open adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") types connect to which MBON types, one can examine the subclasses of MBONs, of which VFB has [69](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of MBON") records, and the subclasses of adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons, of which VFB has [21](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") records. 

VFB does not currently hold specific data on the exact connections between the different types of adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons and MBONs in the provided data. However, the available upstream and downstream connectivity classes for both MBONs and adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons can be used to explore their connections further.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type is known to be a type of neuron in the fly brain. According to VFB, it detects looming stimuli and its activity elicits a jump escape response. The cell body of LPLC2 lies in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind. VFB records show that LPLC2 has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, allowing it to detect looming stimuli. VFB does not currently hold detailed information on the specific connections of LPLC2 to other neurons. For more information on LPLC2, including its connections and function, the user can query the VFB database directly.

results.title: Bidirectional connectivity
results.question: Are there reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) and dopaminergic neurons (DANs)? Which pairs have the strongest mutual connectivity?
results.response:
The connectome data indicates that there are reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons and dopaminergic neurons. VFB records show 22 reciprocal class-level pairs between these two neuron types. The total weight of connections from mushroom body output neurons to dopaminergic neurons is 7620, and from dopaminergic neurons to mushroom body output neurons is 2697. 

VFB has annotated a large number of connectivity records for both mushroom body output neurons and dopaminergic neurons, including [2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") downstream and [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") upstream connectivity classes for mushroom body output neurons, and [8845](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for dopaminergic neuron") downstream and [7914](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for dopaminergic neuron") upstream connectivity classes for dopaminergic neurons. 

To identify the specific pairs with the strongest mutual connectivity, you can explore the downstream and upstream connectivity classes for both mushroom body output neurons and dopaminergic neurons, and examine the pairwise connections and total weights for each pair. VFB holds a substantial amount of data on these neuron types, including images, subclasses, scRNAseq data, and transgene expression data, which may provide further insights into their connectivity and function.

results.title: Pathway tracing
results.question: Trace a pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the lateral horn. What are the intermediate neuron types and their connections?
results.response:
To trace a pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the [adult lateral horn](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007053 "Open adult lateral horn in Virtual Fly Brain"), we can look at the intermediate neuron types and their connections. According to VFB, a high-level pathway is [olfactory receptor neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005926 "Open olfactory receptor neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") -> antennal lobe projection neuron -> adult lateral horn. 

VFB holds data on downstream connectivity classes for olfactory receptor neuron, with [575](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005926,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for olfactory receptor neuron") records, and upstream connectivity classes, with [379](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005926,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for olfactory receptor neuron") records. For the adult lateral horn, VFB has annotated neurons with some part in this region ([1661](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00007053,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in adult lateral horn") records), neurons with synaptic terminals ([1658](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00007053,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in adult lateral horn") records), and neurons with presynaptic and postsynaptic terminals. 

The connectome data indicates that antennal lobe projection neurons receive olfactory input in the antennal lobe and send axons to higher brain centers, including the adult lateral horn. 

For more detailed information on the specific connections and neuron types involved, you can explore the available VFB data, such as the images of olfactory receptor neuron ([19014](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005926,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of olfactory receptor neuron") records), scRNAseq data for olfactory receptor neuron ([96](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005926,anatScRNAseqQuery "Run in VFB: scRNAseq data for olfactory receptor neuron") records), and transgene expression in adult lateral horn ([1935](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00007053,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in adult lateral horn") records).

results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?
results.response:
The containment hierarchy from the [antennal lobe glomerulus DA1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003932 "Open antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 in Virtual Fly Brain") up to the top-level brain structure is: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult olfactory antennal lobe glomerulus, or alternatively, antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum, or further, antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain, as indicated by VFB. Each level in the hierarchy represents a brain structure that contains the previous one. 

VFB holds data on the antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, including neurons with some part in it, neurons with synaptic terminals in it, images of neurons with some part in it, and transgene expression in it. 

To further explore the hierarchy, you can query VFB for the parent structures of each level, or examine the images and neuron data available for the antennal lobe glomerulus DA1.

results.title: Cross-region connectivity
results.question: What neuron types connect the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe, and how strong are these connections?
results.response:
The neuron types that connect the [adult central complex](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003632 "Open adult central complex in Virtual Fly Brain") to the [lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_00050314 "Open lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018 in Virtual Fly Brain") include larval mushroom body output neurons and larval dopaminergic neurons, specifically [larval mushroom body output neuron f2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047974 "Open larval mushroom body output neuron f2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [larval mushroom body output neuron m1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047988 "Open larval mushroom body output neuron m1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [larval dopaminergic DM1b neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110928 "Open larval dopaminergic DM1b neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), as recorded in VFB. Additionally, VFB records show that other neuron types connecting the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe are PFL1, PFL2_PB4, PFL3_PB7, PFL1_PB1, PFL1_PB7, and PFL1_PB2. 

The strength of these connections is not specified in the available evidence. VFB holds numerous records of neurons with some part in, or synaptic terminals in, both the adult central complex and the lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018, which may provide further insight into the connectivity between these regions.

results.title: Experimental planning
results.question: I want to study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. What neurons are involved, how are they connected, and what genetic tools can I use to access them?
results.response:
To study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, we need to identify the neurons involved, their connections, and the genetic tools available to access them. VFB does not currently hold specific data on the neural circuit for CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. However, it is known from the literature that certain neurons, such as those expressing the Gr21a and Gr63a receptors, are involved in CO2 detection (e.g., as reported by Jones et al., 2007, and also Suh et al., 2004). 

The connectome data indicates that these neurons are likely connected to other neurons in the antennal lobe and the ventral nerve cord, but the exact connectivity is not specified in the available VFB data. 

For accessing these neurons genetically, tools such as the Gal4/UAS system can be used, which allows for targeted expression of genes in specific neurons (Brand and Perrimon, 1993). However, the specific Gal4 lines that target the CO2-avoidance neurons are not annotated in the available VFB data. 

To further investigate the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance, you can query the VFB database for neurons expressing specific receptors or genes, and explore their connections and genetic accessibility. Additionally, you can search for publications that have studied the CO2 avoidance behavior in Drosophila and characterized the involved neural circuits. 

References:
Brand, A. H., & Perrimon, N. (1993). Targeted gene expression as a means of altering cell fates and generating dominant phenotypes. Development, 118(2), 401-415.
Jones, W. D., Cayirlioglu, P., Grunwald Kadow, I., & Vosshall, L. B. (2007). Two chemosensory receptors together mediate carbon dioxide detection in Drosophila. Nature, 445(7123), 86-90.
Suh, G. S., Wong, A. M., Hergarden, A. C., Wang, J. W., Simon, A. F., Benzer, S., ... & Anderson, D. J. (2004). A single population of olfactory sensory neurons mediates an innate avoidance behaviour in Drosophila. Nature, 431(7010), 854-859.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, as noted in the work by Thomas and Wyman, 1984. VFB records show that the giant fiber neuron has a distinct anatomy and connectivity. 

VFB holds [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") records of images of the giant fiber neuron, specifically of DNp01, and [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01. The downstream connectivity classes for DNp01 are represented by [361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records, while the upstream connectivity classes for DNp01 are represented by [435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records. 

The giant fiber neuron's involvement in jump escape behavior is documented, with the neuron playing a key role in this process. Available driver lines for the giant fiber neuron are not specified in the provided evidence, but the existing records on transgene expression may provide insights into tools available for its study. 

Relevant publications, such as the one by Thomas and Wyman, 1984, provide more information on the giant fiber neuron's anatomy, connectivity, and function. For a comprehensive understanding, consulting these publications and exploring the available VFB data is recommended.

results.title: Hypothesis generation
results.question: Based on connectivity data, what neuron types might mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body? Could visual information reach the memory circuit?
results.response:
Based on connectivity data, several neuron types might mediate a connection between the [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain"). VFB records show that neurons such as [CB2311](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20005873 "Open CB2311 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [CB2443](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20005995 "Open CB2443 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [CB3379](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20006842 "Open CB3379 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [MB-C2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100228 "Open MB-C2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [MB-M1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100229 "Open MB-M1 in Virtual Fly Brain") have some part in the mushroom body, and could potentially connect the visual system to the mushroom body. Additionally, neurons with some part in the visual system, including [ML-VPN2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052139 "Open ML-VPN2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052141 "Open Mt-VPN1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052140 "Open Mt-VPN in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mti](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052142 "Open Mti in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [T4ai neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052241 "Open T4ai neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), might also play a role in this connection. Furthermore, VFB data indicates that adult visual projection neurons have presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body, suggesting they may mediate the connection between the visual system and the mushroom body. 

VFB holds numerous records related to both the visual system and the mushroom body, including [1046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in visual system") neurons with some part in the visual system, [982](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in visual system") neurons with synaptic terminals in the visual system, and [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") neurons with some part in the mushroom body. These data suggest that visual information could potentially reach the memory circuit via connections between the visual system and the mushroom body. 

To further explore the connection between the visual system and the mushroom body, one could examine the specific neuron types and their synaptic terminals, as well as the parts and subclasses of the mushroom body, and the tracts and nerves that innervate it, all of which are available in VFB.

results.title: Comparative analysis
results.question: Compare the downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons (s-LNv and l-LNv). Do they converge on any common target neuron types?
results.response: The downstream targets of [s-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch03yp "Open s-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain") and [l-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fws "Open l-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain") have been compared, and VFB records show that they share 17 common downstream target classes. These shared targets include adult cholinergic neuron, adult octopaminergic neuron, adult serotonergic neuron, and various types of adult neurons, such as adult CA-LP neuron, adult CB3698 neuron, and adult optic lobe neuron. Additionally, they also converge on interneurons, sensory system neurons, and visual system neurons. The connectome data indicates that these clock neurons have overlapping downstream targets, suggesting potential convergence of their outputs. VFB holds these 17 shared downstream target classes among the compared source classes.

results.response:

VFB holds [2698](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in subesophageal zone") records of neurons with some part in the subesophageal zone, including examples such as [CB0550](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20004300 "Open CB0550 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [CB0552](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20004301 "Open CB0552 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [DSOG2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047702 "Open DSOG2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [IB097](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20001274 "Open IB097 in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [SMP586](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20003448 "Open SMP586 in Virtual Fly Brain"). Regarding connectomics data, VFB has neurons with some part in the subesophageal zone, and these can include image-backed connectome or light-microscopy examples. 

For genetic tools, VFB returned 4205 genetic tool/expression pattern rows for the subesophageal zone, which includes GAL4 drivers and binary/intersectional drivers. 

VFB also holds [1](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,ExpressionOverlapsHere "Run in VFB: Expression patterns overlapping subesophageal zone") record of an expression pattern overlapping the subesophageal zone and 1 record of transgene expression in the subesophageal zone. 

To further explore the subesophageal zone, you can query VFB for more specific information on its neuron types, connectomics data, and genetic tools.
